title: After Makkah, the Wind of Arabia • The Shadow of Rome • This Time, Naming the Destination • The Race of Giving • Those Without Mounts • The Day of Departure, ‘Ali’s Hurt • The Hardship of the Road • Past al-Hijr • The Spring of Tabuk • The Romans Did Not Come

blocks.0: After Makkah, the Wind of Arabia
blocks.1: Makkah has been conquered. The battles of Hunayn and Ta’if are over. A new wind is now blowing across the heart of Arabia. The tribes that had been sitting far away watching, to see who would win the fight between Quraysh and Muhammad, now find nothing left to watch. People have begun coming into the shade of Islam in crowds. Ten years of unbroken fighting. Badr, Uhud, the Trench, Khaybar, Makkah, Hunayn. For the first time the people of Madinah have found a chance to catch their breath. They have returned home, put their hands to their orchards, and begun counting up the harvest to bring in. But one thorn still remained, the farthest, the biggest. Rome. A year earlier, on the plain of Mu’tah, three thousand Muslims had stood before the vast army of Rome. Three commanders had been martyred. By the strategy of Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA) the army had come back. But the emperor of Rome, Caesar Heraclius, could not forget that event. To him it was now not merely a battle, but a danger on the frontier. If the tribes of Arabia that have begun to speak of independence hear this story of Rome’s humiliation, who will guard Rome’s borders?{{1}}
blocks.2: The Messenger of Allah {{1}} understood all of this. He had no room to sit back in the joy of the conquest of Makkah. The danger ahead had to be stopped before it reached the door.
blocks.4: In the air of Madinah there was only one talk then. That Ghassan was shoeing its horses. In every home in Madinah there was this fear. ‘Umar (RA) has said,
blocks.5: We used to say among ourselves that Ghassan was shoeing its horses to attack us.{{1}}
blocks.6: The fear was not baseless. The Nabataean merchants who came to Madinah from Syria bringing oil brought news. Heraclius had gathered a monstrous army of forty thousand soldiers. He had paid the soldiers a year’s salary in advance. With them the Arab Christian tribes of Lakhm and Judham. At the head of the army, famous commanders of Rome. Their advance party had already reached Balqa’. That very day a terror spread through Madinah that no one could forget, day or night. At any unfamiliar sound it seemed that the Romans had arrived.{{1}}
blocks.7: And inside Madinah, the time was the most difficult of all. After ten years of continuous war, a little peace had come for the first time. The dates were ripening, and on these dates rested the livelihood of the people of Madinah for the whole year. Leaving the orchards was not easy. The heat of Arabia was fierce then. It felt as if fire rained from the sky, sparks leapt from the ground. The journey too was very long. Nearly eight hundred miles, mostly harsh desert. Mounts were few. And as for the Romans they were to face, the Muslims had no idea at all of their methods of warfare.{{1}}
blocks.8: And the time was the most difficult of all. Ka‘b ibn Malik (RA) has spoken of those days,
blocks.9: The Prophet {{1}} set out on this expedition in the midst of fierce heat. Ahead lay a distant journey, endless desert, and an enormous number of enemies.{{2}}
blocks.10: The Prophet {{1}} calculated. If the Romans came to Madinah first, then all the spread that Islam had gained through years of toil and sweat would be wasted in an instant. After the storm of Hunayn, Jahiliyyah, thrashing on its deathbed, would take courage again. And the hypocrites within, who until now had been sitting with daggers in hand behind the back, would join hands with the Romans and plunge the knife into the back. So the decision was made: before they come, we will go.{{2}}
blocks.11: Some tasks are never done if one waits for good days. Let the heat ease, let the harvest come in, let the road become easy, let companions increase; such a day does not come.
blocks.13: The Prophet’s {{1}} rule was to conceal the destination before setting out for battle. He would be going in one direction and speak of another. This time he did not do so. Ka‘b (RA) says,
blocks.14: The Prophet {{1}} laid the matter openly before the Muslims, so that they could make full preparation. He also told them which direction he was going.{{2}}
blocks.15: The Companions were so many that not everyone’s name was written in any register. Ka‘b (RA) says,
blocks.16: Whoever wished to stay absent would think that unless revelation from Allah came, the matter would remain hidden.{{1}}
blocks.17: The announcement to prepare for war went out in every direction. To the other tribes of Arabia, to the people of Makkah too. At this time a part of Surah al-Tawbah was revealed. The Muslims were urged to jihad. The Prophet {{1}} encouraged them to spend the best part of their wealth in the way of Allah.{{2}}
blocks.18: The Qur’an puts that call this way,
blocks.20: O believers! What is the matter with you that when you were told to go out in the way of Allah, you became weighed down and clung to the earth? Are you content with the life of this world in place of the Hereafter? (If so, then remember) against the Hereafter the enjoyment of this worldly life is very little.{{1}}
blocks.21: And what will happen if they do not go, the Qur’an has said at once,
blocks.23: If you do not go out, Allah will punish you with a painful punishment and will bring another people in your place, and you cannot harm Him in the least. Allah has complete power over all things.{{1}}
blocks.24: And the call to go had come for everyone, with no exemption to sit at home, in every state, light or heavy. The Qur’an puts that call this way,
blocks.26: (Set out for jihad) go forth, whether you are light or heavy, and strive with your lives and wealth in the way of Allah. If you have understanding, this is better for you.{{1}}
blocks.27: As for those who stood behind the shield of excuses, the Qur’an has also pulled out what was in their hearts: had the road been near and the profit in hand, these very people would have walked first of all.
blocks.29: Had there been immediate worldly gain in sight and the journey been of moderate length, they (that is, the hypocrites) would surely have followed you. But this hard road seemed too far to them. Now they will swear by Allah, saying, if we had been able, we would surely have gone out with you. They are destroying themselves, and Allah knows well that they are liars.{{1}}
blocks.30: Before setting out on the desert road, the biggest obstacle is not the enemy but the pull of the earth. ‘Weighed down and clung to the earth,’ this picture of the Qur’an we recognise. Bed, shade, comfort pin us to the ground too.
blocks.32: The call has come, now the preparation. An army of thirty thousand had to be assembled. The Muslims had never before set out with so large a force, and yet mounts were few, provisions few, weapons few. That is why in history this army is named Jaysh al-‘Usrah, the Army of Hardship. And to bear that hardship a race of giving broke out in Madinah. ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah (RA) says, while the army was being equipped ‘Uthman (RA) came with a thousand dinars. He poured them into the lap of the Prophet {{1}}. ‘Abd al-Rahman (RA) says,
blocks.33: I saw the Prophet {{1}} turning the dinars over and over in his lap and saying, after today, whatever ‘Uthman does, no harm will come to him. He said it twice.{{2}}
blocks.34: This is not a licence for sin. It is a declaration of trust in one who knows how to pour out everything for Allah. ‘Umar (RA) says, the Prophet {{1}} commanded sadaqah. That day I had some wealth in my hand. I said to myself, if I can ever surpass Abu Bakr, it is today. I brought half of my wealth. The Prophet {{2}} asked, what have you left for your family? I said, the same amount. Then Abu Bakr came with everything he had.
blocks.35: The Prophet {{1}} asked, Abu Bakr, what have you left for your family? He said, I have left Allah and His Messenger for them.{{2}}
blocks.36: ‘Umar (RA) said, by Allah, I will never be able to surpass him in anything. And those who had nothing at all to give? Abu Mas‘ud (RA) says,
blocks.37: When we were commanded to give sadaqah, we used to labour for wages, carrying loads on our backs. Abu ‘Aqil came with half a sa‘. Another came with more than that. The hypocrites said, Allah has no need of this one’s sadaqah; and that man has brought it only to show off.{{1}}
blocks.38: The Qur’an answered them this way,
blocks.40: (Such hypocrites are) those who find fault with the believers who give sadaqah willingly, and also with those who find nothing but the fruit of their own labour. For this they ridicule them. Allah ridicules them in return. For them a painful punishment is prepared.{{1}}
blocks.41: For the big giver the excuse of ‘showing off,’ and for the small giver the excuse of ‘trivial,’ is always ready. The one who gives nothing, his mouth runs the most. The real bargain behind this giving the Qur’an has put this way,
blocks.43: In fact Allah has bought from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for the Garden being theirs. They fight in the way of Allah, so they kill and are killed. This is a true promise, which Allah has taken upon Himself in the Torah and the Injil, and in the Qur’an too. And who is more faithful to his promise than Allah? So rejoice in the bargain you have made with Allah, and that is the great success.{{1}}
blocks.44: Those who poured out everything that day knew they had not entered a business of loss. They had struck a bargain, whose buyer is Allah.
blocks.46: In the midst of this crowd of giving there was another group, who had nothing to give; they had only the longing to go. No mount had come their way, so they have no excuse, they have yearning. Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari (RA) says, his companions sent him to the Prophet {{1}} to ask for mounts. The Prophet {{2}} was angry at that time, Abu Musa (RA) did not notice. He said,
blocks.47: By Allah, I cannot give you anything to ride.{{1}}
blocks.48: Abu Musa (RA) went back heartbroken. He feared that the Prophet {{1}} might be displeased with him. A little later Bilal (RA) called out, where is ‘Abdullah ibn Qays? The Prophet {{2}} is calling. He went and saw six camels. The Prophet {{3}} said,
blocks.49: These two and these two and these two, six camels in pairs, just bought from Sa‘d. Take them and go to your companions.{{1}}
blocks.50: Allah Himself had drawn the boundary of excuses,
blocks.52: There is no blame on the weak (for not going to jihad), nor on the sick, nor on those who have nothing to spend, as long as they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger. There is no ground of complaint against the doers of good. Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful.{{1}}
blocks.53: And for those who needed this mount, the Qur’an has preserved even their tears,
blocks.55: Nor is there any blame on those who came to you in the hope that you would arrange some mount for them, and you said, I have no mount to give you, whereupon, in grief at having nothing to spend, they turned back with tears flowing from their eyes.{{1}}
blocks.56: They did not weep because they got no mount; they wept because the reward slipped away. Though there would have been no sin on them even if they did not go, their eyes flooded with grief at the lost opportunity. When did our eyes last grow wet for something that no one would have held us to account for if we had not done it?
blocks.58: The preparation was complete. On the day of departure the Prophet {{1}} left ‘Ali (RA) behind in Madinah. ‘Ali’s (RA) heart grew heavy. There was no battle in which he had not stood beside the Prophet {{2}}; only this time was he left behind. The hypocrites taunted, he has been left because he had become a burden.{{3}}
blocks.59: Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (RA) says, ‘Ali (RA) said to the Prophet {{1}},
blocks.60: Are you leaving me among the children and women? The Prophet {{1}} said, are you not pleased that your standing with me will be like the standing of Harun with Musa? Except that there is no prophet after me.{{2}}
blocks.61: Two things in one sentence. One for ‘Ali, of love. The other for the whole ummah, of boundary. The comparison with Harun (AS) is of responsibility, not of prophethood. To make that clear came the last part of the sentence: there is no prophet after me.
blocks.63: The moment they set out on the road, the true face of hardship appeared. Eighteen men took turns on one camel. Driven by hunger they chewed tree leaves, and their lips swelled. When water ran out they slaughtered a camel and drank the water in its belly.{{1}}
blocks.64: At one point the people were faint with hunger. They said to the Prophet {{1}}, allow us to slaughter our camels and eat, and we will use the oil too. The Prophet {{2}} said, do it. Then ‘Umar (RA) came and said,
blocks.65: O Messenger of Allah, if they do this, the mounts will be fewer. Rather, tell them to bring what remains of their food, then pray for blessing upon it. Perhaps Allah will do something through that.{{1}}
blocks.66: A leather dining-cloth was spread. One brought a handful of corn, another a handful of dates, another a piece of bread. Altogether very little. The Prophet {{1}} prayed for blessing. Then he said, fill your vessels. Not a single vessel of the soldiers remained that they had not filled. All ate to their fill, and still food was left over. Then the Prophet {{2}} said,
blocks.67: I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that I am the Messenger of Allah. Any servant who stands before Allah with these two, without doubt, will not be shut out from the Garden.{{1}}
blocks.68: ‘Umar’s (RA) advice is a lesson of crisis. Not lamenting over what is not there, but bringing together what is there in one place. A handful from each; together, the stomach of the whole army.
blocks.70: On the way lay al-Hijr. The settlement of Thamud, the people of Salih (AS). Those who had built houses by cutting into the mountains. Ibn ‘Umar (RA) says, as they passed there the Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.71: Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves; lest what happened to them happen to you too. But if you enter weeping, that is another matter.{{1}}
blocks.72: Today we go to see ancient ruins. We take photos, laugh, sit down and open food packets. The Prophet {{1}} walked on, his head covered with his cloak.
blocks.74: Coming near Tabuk the Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.75: Tomorrow, in sha’ Allah, you will reach the spring of Tabuk. But not before midday. Whoever arrives first, until I come let him not put his hand in the water there.{{1}}
blocks.76: Mu‘adh (RA) says, when we arrived we found two had already got there. The spring was thin as a shoelace, water seeping out drop by drop. The Prophet {{1}} asked, did you touch its water? They said, yes. He rebuked them. Then the people, filling their cupped hands, gathered a little water bit by bit in a vessel. The Prophet {{2}} washed his face and hands in it, then poured the water back into the spring.
blocks.77: The spring poured out water in a rush, or he said, a great deal of water. The people drank. Then the Prophet {{1}} said, Mu‘adh, if you live long, you will see this place filled with gardens.{{2}}
blocks.78: Another warning of that same night. Abu Humayd al-Sa‘idi (RA) says, on reaching Tabuk the Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.79: Tonight a fierce wind will blow. Let no one stand up. Whoever has a camel with him, let him tie it down.{{1}}
blocks.80: We tied down our camels. At night a fierce wind came. One man stood up. The wind lifted him and threw him down on the mountain of the Tayy tribe. The reason for the order about the spring’s water, ‘do not touch it until I come,’ became clear later. The Prophet’s {{1}} displeasure toward those who had touched it first also says, an order has a reason. The reason is not always understood at once.
blocks.82: The army pitched camp on the plain of Tabuk. The Prophet {{1}} gave a speech; much in few words. He called to the good of this world and the Hereafter, gave warning too, gave glad tidings too. The morale of the Muslim army rose still higher. Meanwhile when the Romans heard that the Prophet {{2}} had arrived with an army of thirty thousand, fear wrapped itself around them like a snake. No one advanced. They scattered and dispersed inside their own country.{{3}}
blocks.83: There was no battle. But the fruits of this silent victory came one after another. The ruler of Aylah, Yuhanna ibn Ru’bah, came and made a treaty, agreed to pay jizyah. The people of Jarba’ and Adhruh also came and paid jizyah. The Prophet {{1}} gave Yuhanna a letter. It began, this is a memorial of peace. On sea and land, the responsibility for their boats and caravans lies with Allah and His Prophet. Abu Humayd (RA) says,
blocks.84: The king of Aylah presented the Prophet {{1}} with a white mule, put a cloak on him, and the Prophet {{2}} gave him a written agreement for their seacoast.{{3}}
blocks.85: Meanwhile Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA) set out with four hundred and twenty horsemen toward Ukaydir, the ruler of Dumat al-Jandal. As he went the Prophet {{1}} said, you will find him hunting a nilgai (blue bull). On a moonlit night a nilgai was rubbing its horns on the palace gate. Ukaydir went out to hunt. Khalid (RA) seized him and brought him to the Prophet {{2}}. In return for his life he gave two thousand camels, eight hundred helmets, four hundred coats of mail and four hundred spears, along with an acknowledgement of jizyah.{{3}}
blocks.86: Not every victory comes by the sword. Sometimes victory means the enemy not coming forward. Standing firm is then the work itself.

footnotes.32: Sahih al-Bukhari 1481 (‘wa-kataba lahu bi-bahrihim’). The detailed text of the letter is sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 709. The accounts of the treaties with Yuhanna ibn Ru’bah, Jarba’–Adhruh and Mina (a quarter of the fruit) are also sirah-based.
footnotes.33: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 709–710 (Khalid (RA)’s four hundred and twenty horsemen; ‘you will find him hunting a nilgai’; Ukaydir granted his life, two thousand camels, eight hundred helmets, four hundred coats of mail, four hundred spears; the treaties of Dumah, Tabuk, Aylah, Taymah). Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.

quiz.q: At the sound of knocking, what was the first question that came from ‘Umar (RA)’s mouth?
o: Have you been able to recognise them?
Have you ever seen a diamond?

quiz.q: According to the news from the Syrian merchants, how many soldiers had Heraclius gathered?
Why did the Prophet ﷺ decide on the expedition even in the harshest heat?
o: The dates were ripening and the shade of Madinah was cool
The soldiers were tired and gloomy because of the lack of mounts
Had they entered Madinah, eight years of achievement would have been shaken
The hypocrites had asked for permission, and so the call came

quiz.q: Breaking the usual rule, what did the Prophet ﷺ do this time about the destination?
o: Concealed it by speaking of another direction
Sent a herald to tell them to avoid the mountain pass
Forbade going to the spring before midday
Opened up and told the Muslims

quiz.q: The Qur’an says of the hypocrites that if the road were near and the gain immediate, they would have followed. Which is their problem in this?
o: Reluctance of heart toward a hard, distant road
The grief of not finding a mount
The disapproval and obstruction of relatives at home

quiz.q: How many dinars did ‘Uthman (RA) pour into the lap of the Prophet ﷺ?
To the question ‘What have you left for your family?’ what answer did Abu Bakr (RA) give?
o: Wealth equal to half of his own
quiz.e: Tirmidhi 3675. ‘The same amount’ was ‘Umar’s answer; the share of Khaybar is Ka‘b’s; the six camels are Abu Musa’s.

quiz.q: Which Companion had brought half a sa‘?
quiz.e: Bukhari 4668. Abu Mas‘ud is its narrator.

quiz.q: Which is the correct explanation of ‘After today, whatever ‘Uthman does, no harm will come to him’?
o: Giving a direct permit to commit sins
A declaration belittling the donations of the other Companions
A declaration that the accounting of giving ended right there
A declaration of trust in a man who pours out everything

quiz.q: A poor student has given a little to the mosque’s fund, and someone is mocking. To which incident of the dars does this scene correspond?
o: Ka‘b’s keeping his share of Khaybar

quiz.q: Two friends compete in good deeds, one always ahead. What does the incident of ‘Umar and Abu Bakr (RA) teach?
o: If you lose, you must quit the competition
Giving everything to stay ahead is the rule
Competition is improper even in good deeds
There is joy even in losing to the friend who is ahead

quiz.q: From whom were the six camels that the Prophet ﷺ gave Abu Musa (RA) bought?
What was the real cause of the tears of the Companions who turned back without finding a mount?
o: Fear of the Prophet’s ﷺ anger
Grief at the reward slipping away

quiz.q: By saying ‘Are you not pleased…’ what comparison did the Prophet ﷺ give ‘Ali (RA)?
o: The standing of Harun with Musa
The keeper of the Messenger’s secrets
The first to rush up with congratulations

quiz.q: What does the sentence ‘Except that there is no prophet after me’ do?
o: Orders ‘Ali to stay longer in Madinah
Separates the comparison with Harun from prophethood and keeps it in responsibility
Shares the standing of prophethood with ‘Ali too

quiz.q: How many soldiers took turns on one camel?
When permission was sought to slaughter the camels, who stopped it and advised blessing?
In an organisation food is short, and everyone is despondent. According to ‘Umar (RA)’s advice, what should be done?
o: Put away whatever each has and wait for fresh help
Gather what is there and pray for blessing
Slaughter all the mounts there are
Not even try to ask anyone for anything

quiz.q: Al-Hijr is the settlement of the people of which prophet?
A tourist goes to a destroyed ancient settlement, taking photos and laughing. What lesson comes from the Prophet’s ﷺ conduct?
o: Stop at the settlement and look around every house
Drink the water of its well there to your fill
Arrange to spend the night inside the settlement
Pass quickly with head covered, weeping

quiz.q: In whose narration is the hadith of the spring of Tabuk?
quiz.e: Muslim 706. Abu Humayd narrated the hadith of the wind, Taba and Uhud; Ibn ‘Umar that of al-Hijr; Abu Musa that of the mounts.

quiz.q: Where did the wind throw the man who stood up on the night of the fierce wind?
o: On the mountain of the Tayy tribe
On the peak of Mount Uhud
On the peak of Mount Sal‘

quiz.q: What can be learned from the Prophet’s ﷺ order about touching the spring’s water and the violation by two men?
o: Every order must be obeyed only after knowing its reason in advance
The first to reach water has a right over it
Storing water on a journey is entirely forbidden
An order has a reason, which is not always understood at once

quiz.q: What gift did the king of Aylah give the Prophet ﷺ?
quiz.e: Bukhari 1481. The six camels are Abu Musa’s, the date-palm branch is the one before Musaylamah, the two thousand camels are Ukaydir’s.

quiz.q: With how many horsemen did Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA) go to Dumat al-Jandal?
How is the absence of fighting at Tabuk viewed?
o: The enemy’s not advancing is also a victory
The hardship of eight hundred miles going to waste
The purpose of the journey failing
